vignette: Arthur sits across from me, his hands resting lightly on the arms of the chair. At seventy, he still dresses with the same careful attention he brings to client meetings-pressed slacks, a watch that ticks with quiet precision, a posture that says he means business. But lately, that business feels like armor. He works as a salesperson who still makes his rounds, still closes deals, but the rhythm of his days has shifted. The silence in his car between appointments stretches longer now. He drives past the places that feel too familiar, charts alternate routes without telling his wife, Elena, why. He tells me about a night six years ago, but the memory unfolds in his mind with the same sharp clarity as if it happens today. It is a rainy Tuesday behind a motel parking lot. A man who starts as a customer and becomes a threat. One moment it is just a negotiation over floor samples; the next, a fist connects with his ribs, followed by the sharp crack of a knee in his gut. Arthur goes down in the wet asphalt. He remembers the smell of damp concrete, the frantic scramble to get up, the way the attacker's breath smells of peppermint and rage before the police sirens finally cut through the dark. There is no weapon drawn, just a sudden, brutal escalation that leaves his body braced for the next strike. In the months that follow, Arthur tries to return to his old routine. Sales demands presence, and presence demands trust. But trust becomes a currency he cannot spend. During presentations, he finds himself tracking the exits before he ever looks at the client's face. He rehearses conversations in his head until they feel like scripts, not conversations. When a man leans across a conference table to shake his hand, Arthur's breath catches, his palms go damp, and he pulls back just a fraction too fast. He tells himself he is just getting older, but Elena notices the way he flinches at heavy footsteps in the hallway, the way he checks the locks three times before bed, the way he sleeps with one eye open and the other toward the door. They walk long stretches after dinner. Now, he says he is tired, that he prefers to sit in the quiet of his study, where the shadows behave predictably. In session, Arthur speaks in a measured cadence, the same tone he uses to negotiate with difficult buyers. He does not describe symptoms; he describes logistics. He talks about the extra hour he spends driving home to avoid downtown. He mentions how he now sits facing the wall during client lunches so he can watch the room. He laughs sometimes, a dry sound, and says he loves the unpredictability of sales. Now he craves it less, not because he has lost his passion for the work, but because his body has decided the world is a place that lunges from the corners. A recent questionnaire places his score at thirty-five, but he does not hear numbers when he talks to me. He hears the rain from that night, feels the familiar tightening in his chest when a chair scrapes against the floor, and wonders if this is how aging feels-like carrying a live wire under his skin. He leaves each session with the same deliberate pace he arrives with, nodding politely, thanking me for listening. Outside, the wind picks up, rattling the windowpanes. Arthur adjusts his coat, checks the side mirror before walking to his car, and starts the engine. He does it all with the quiet determination of a man who has learned to survive, still moving forward, still showing up, carrying the weight of a night that never really ends, but learning, session by session, how to stand in the daylight without flinching quite as hard.
